name: Fuel Metabolism: The Feed-Fast Cycle, Hepatic Ketogenesis, and Diabetic Ketoacidosis

reference.source: Medical Biochemistry 5th ed / Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry 8th ed
clinicalPearls: In the well-fed state, high insulin drives glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and GLUT4-mediated glucose entry into muscle and fat
Fasting hepatic glycogen depletes within 24 hours, after which gluconeogenesis sustains blood glucose from alanine, lactate, and glycerol
In starvation, oxaloacetate is consumed for gluconeogenesis, diverting excess beta-oxidation acetyl-CoA into ketogenesis
Ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) supply up to two-thirds of cerebral energy requirements in prolonged starvation
Diabetic ketoacidosis features severe insulin lack, high counter-regulatory hormones, high anion gap acidosis, and osmotic diuresis
reference.pathophysiology: The feed-fast transition is orchestrated by the insulin-to-glucagon ratio. When insulin is absent or low, adipose hormone-sensitive lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides, releasing free fatty acids. Hepatic beta-oxidation saturates the TCA cycle; depleted oxaloacetate forces excess acetyl-CoA into HMG-CoA synthase-mediated synthesis of acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. In DKA, uncontrolled acid accumulation exhausts plasma bicarbonate buffers, generating severe high anion gap ketoacidosis.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) vs Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)
Alcoholic ketoacidosis (depleted glycogen + elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio)
Starvation ketosis (mild acidosis, normal or low glucose)
additionalInvestigations: Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate quantitative assay (superior to urine dipstick for acetoacetate)
Arterial or venous blood gas (pH < 7.30, HCO3 < 18 mEq/L in DKA)
Serum electrolytes, calculated anion gap, and plasma glucose
Serum and urine osmolality, and hourly bedside glucose monitoring
